The guidelines for conducting HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending antenatal clinics (ANC) are a joint effort by WHO and UNAIDS. This document is based on country experiences and expert reviews from WHO, UNAIDS, and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The development of this document was coordinated by WHO and CDC, with significant technical input from experts at WHO, CDC, Imperial College London, and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. Additional technical reviews were provided by experts from various institutions, including national public health organizations in Zambia, Kenya, Ethiopia, and Nigeria. The findings, conclusions, and recommendations in this report reflect the views of WHO and UNAIDS and do not necessarily represent the official position of the CDC. Funding for this work was provided by the US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), UNAIDS, and WHO. The purpose of this guidance document is to assist national HIV surveillance program staff in monitoring trends in their country’s HIV epidemics. It describes how routine data from prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs can be used for HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC. These guidelines assume that surveillance programs have already assessed the readiness of routine program data for surveillance purposes, as outlined in WHO’s 2013 guidelines for assessing PMTCT program data utility for HIV sentinel surveillance. The technical guidance in this document covers surveillance design and implementation, site selection, sample size calculation, data collection, analysis and interpretation, monitoring, and dissemination of results. It is based on input from surveillance experts and lessons learned from the field. Countries are encouraged to adopt or adapt this guidance as appropriate. HIV surveillance among pregnant women in the context of second-generation surveillance is critical for understanding the epidemic. Countries require HIV prevalence data to monitor the epidemic’s trajectory, allocate resources, and plan and evaluate interventions. Over the past two decades, ANC-based HIV surveillance has provided valuable insights into the burden and trends of HIV prevalence among pregnant women. Historically, this surveillance has been conducted using unlinked anonymous testing (UAT). ANC settings provide an accessible cross-section of healthy, sexually active women in the general population. Despite recognized limitations and biases, HIV surveillance estimates from ANC can serve as a useful proxy for trends in the general female population. Routine program data for HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC has become increasingly viable due to improvements in HIV prevention and treatment programs. These include expanded access to diagnostic HIV testing in ANC settings, higher coverage of PMTCT and antiretroviral therapy (ART) programs, and the transition to immediate, lifelong ART (Option B+) for HIV-positive pregnant women. In 2014, approximately 50% of pregnant women in lowand middle-income countries received an HIV test and their results. Additionally, an estimated 73% of HIV-positive pregnant women in these countries received ART to prevent mother-to-child transmission. As programs expand and strengthen, routine program data can increasingly provide demographic, HIV, and syphilis data previously captured by UAT-based serosurveillance. Routine data collection offers several advantages, including reduced resource requirements, expanded surveillance coverage, and support for sustainable surveillance efforts. It also fosters a culture of using routine data for surveillance, benefiting service delivery and program monitoring. HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC based on routine program data relies on effective functioning, monitoring, quality assurance, and strengthening of inputs and activities managed by multiple programs. These include maternal and child health (MCH) or PMTCT programs, national reference laboratories, central medical stores, health management information systems (HMIS), and electronic medical record (EMR) systems. Surveillance based on routine program data should be a collaborative effort, engaging programmatic partners early and often. Identified gaps or challenges in data quality or HIV testing should inform system-strengthening measures. All surveillance activities, including HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC, must adhere to ethical principles of biomedical research and surveillance. These principles include respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. Protocols for HIV surveillance should be reviewed and approved by relevant ethical review boards before implementation. Informed consent is not required for surveillance based on routine program data, as all data come from standard clinical practice. Safeguards must be in place to protect the rights, welfare, and confidentiality of pregnant women whose data are collected for surveillance. Surveillance design should ensure reliable epidemiological data while being resource-efficient. Census-based approaches, using individual-level data from verified EMR systems or aggregate data from HMIS, are preferred for their resource efficiency and comprehensive geographic coverage. However, many countries may not yet be ready to implement census-based approaches due to challenges with EMR and HMIS systems. Sentinel surveillance design remains a viable alternative, and this document provides guidance on its implementation. Surveillance programs should define the variables to be collected for HIV surveillance among pregnant women attending ANC. All necessary variables for appropriate epidemiological analyses should be selected, ensuring the collection of accurate and comprehensive data.
